images.title: Hôtel privé, 8 rue de Valois-du-Roule — élévation principale
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architects Nolau et Convents; engraver J. Penel
images.shows: Full principal elevation, 'Hôtel privé, Première Classe': straight 45° mansard comble with pedimented dormers and cresting, running wrought-iron balconies at two floors, rusticated ground floor, flat wall plane in pierre de taille, printed metric scale bar for direct measurement.

images.title: Hôtel privé, 8 rue de Turin — croisées du rez-de-chaussée (détail mesuré)
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. Brouty; engraver Sulpis
images.shows: Large-scale measured detail of a ground-floor window bay with full dimension callouts in metres: bossage coursing on the socle, wrought-iron balcon-garde-corps scrollwork, entablature and pediment mouldings — a plate answerable to exact proportions rather than a photograph's estimate.

images.title: Hôtel privé, 17 rue Vanneau — élévation principale
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. E. Petit; engraver Lebel
images.shows: Textbook narrow street-front elevation, 'Deuxième Classe': straight comble with three pedimented dormers, continuous cast-iron balconies at two floors, flat unadorned ashlar wall plane, ground-floor door and barred windows — the canonical narrow haussmannien house front with printed metric scale.

images.title: Hôtel privé, 17 rue Vanneau — élévation postérieure (façade sur cour)
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. E. Petit; engraver Lebel
images.shows: Companion rear/courtyard elevation of the same house: plainer treatment than the street front, still with balconies and a straight comble at every floor, showing how the classical street facade contrasts with the working courtyard face of an identical structure.

images.title: Maison à loyer, avenue de l'Impératrice — coupe générale
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. Raban; engraver Bordet
images.street: avenue de l'Impératrice (today avenue Foch), Paris
images.shows: Full building section ('coupe générale') cut through the porte-cochère passage: interior room heights and decor at left against the exterior street elevation at right, courtyard, and rear service wing — the single plate type in this family that reveals true floor-to-floor heights rather than only the outward face.

images.title: Maison à loyer, 3 rue de la Paix — élévation
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. Paul Mesnard; engraver J. Penel
images.shows: A 'Première Classe' rental building (the standard haussmannien maison à loyer type): ground-floor shopfronts, two full-width running iron balconies (2nd and 5th-floor pattern), straight mansard comble with pedimented dormers, and a flat symmetrical facade plane — the clearest single-plate demonstration of the balcon filant rule.

images.title: Maison à loyer, 120 boulevard de Sébastopol — détails de la façade
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. Levicomte; engraver J. Penel
images.shows: Fully measured entrance-bay detail on the flagship percée boulevard: entresol window and door surround with dimensioned mouldings, balcony-console profile with metric callouts, door hardware — usable for exact proportions of the rez-de-chaussée treatment that a photograph could not supply.

images.title: Maison à loyer, 9 rue du Conservatoire — détail de la façade
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architect M. Amoudru; engraver Sulpis
images.shows: Two stacked measured window bays with cast-iron balcon-filant railings, floral rosette bandeau, and dimensioned mouldings/reveals in metres and centimetres — a second independent source for exact balcony and window proportions.

images.title: Maison à loyer, 63 boulevard de Sébastopol — détail de la façade
images.author: César Daly (publisher); architects MM. Garnier et Coulon; engraver Sulpis
images.shows: Measured door/window-pediment detail with a full dimension ladder in the margin: cartouche carving, bossage coursing either side of the opening, and an arched porte-cochère lintel below — another exact-proportions source for ground-floor surrounds on the same boulevard.

notes: All 9 kept images come from César Daly's 'L'Architecture privée au XIXe siècle sous Napoléon III' (Paris: A. Morel, 1864), Série 1, Volume 1 — individually-scanned page images from an Internet Archive copy, uploaded to Commons under a Flickr-Commons-style batch and confirmed Public Domain via extmetadata. This is the exact source named in the brief and it delivers precisely the material requested: fully dimensioned elevations and one section ('coupe générale'), each captioned with address, architect, and building class (Première/Deuxième/Troisième Classe) by the publisher in 1864 — inside the 1853-1870 window with no dating inferred by us. Two building types recur: 'Hôtel privé' (private townhouse) and 'Maison à loyer' (rental apartment building, the literal haussmannien immeuble); both show the canonical features — straight 45° combles with pedimented dormers, running cast-iron balconies at upper floors, flat ashlar wall planes, and ground-floor bossage — with no bow windows, curved combles, or post-1880s ornament anywhere in the set. Rejects (9): the same Commons search/category surfaced (a) plan-only plates for maisons at 77 and 87 Boulevard de Sébastopol and cellar/sous-sol plans at 88 rue de Rivoli — dropped per brief (plans are out of scope for an ELEVATION family); (b) a door-joinery profile detail (87 Bd Sébastopol) too narrow in subject for this family; (c) Daly's Série 2 Vol. 2 ('Villas, chalets, jardins') and Vol. 3 ('Décorations intérieures') — both confirmed via extmetadata to be villas/interiors, not Paris street immeubles, so skipped wholesale; (d) 'Hôtels privés, 10 et 12 rue Balzac' — grand freestanding townhouses with individual exterior perron staircases, judged too individualised/detached from block-front unity to serve as the canonical example, kept only as a considered pass; (e) several pre-1853 Paris Musées/Gallica hôtel-particulier elevations (Barré, Lecointe, Haudebourt — dated 1735-1835) surfaced by 'Category:Architectural elevations of Paris' were rejected on period grounds before download. Coverage gap: no competition or permit drawing was found meeting both period and legibility bars in the time available — everything here is published-plate material (Daly/Morel), not an administrative permit set; a further pass could search Archives de Paris permis de construire scans specifically. No image required an inferred construction year — all dates are the publisher's own 1864 imprint, and 'grand'/'comfortable' klass calls follow the plates' own Première/Deuxième Classe captions, not a guess.
